_comment: How Egyptian Arabic (Cairene) says the letters a romanisation of standard Arabic writes, for lib/translit.py: read before lib/lang/ar.ipa.json for a book or a video written in Egyptian (variety ar.egy). Whatever this file does not say is ar.ipa.json's. ONLY the consonant correspondences every description of Cairene gives; vowels, endings and stress are not touched (a standard verb's kataba stays kataba, where Cairo says katab).
_sources: Janet C. E. Watson, The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic (Oxford University Press, 2002), ch. 2: Cairene q > ʔ, j > g, the interdentals > stops.
Manfred Woidich, Das Kairenisch-Arabische: eine Grammatik (Harrassowitz, 2006), §1 (Lautlehre).
Kees Versteegh, The Arabic Language, 2nd ed. (Edinburgh University Press, 2014), ch. 10 (the Egyptian dialects).

from_standard._map: A letter of the standard romanisation (lib/lookup.py: the standard dictionary's hits, shown in a text written in Egyptian) to the letter Cairo says. ق is a glottal stop (qalb > ʾalb); ج is g (jamīl > gamīl); ث ذ ظ are t d ḍ (ṯalāṯa > talāta, ḏahab > dahab, ẓuhr > ḍuhr). In words taken from the written language the same letters are said q, s, z, ẓ (qurʾān, ṯawra > sawra): that split is word by word and is left to the research brief, so these are the everyday words' sounds.

roman._keep_initial: The Egyptian dictionary writes a word that begins with ق with its glottal stop (قلب ʔalb): that ʾ is the word's first consonant and is kept, where the hamza of a word that begins with a vowel (أنا ʔana) is dropped as ar.ipa.json says.
